patch.title: How do you build knowledge that survives delay?
patch.content:
Not recognition. Not pages reviewed. Durable learning means reconstructing an idea after time has passed, explaining its mechanism, choosing when it applies, and using it under changed cues.

Delaysurvives time
Transfersurvives change
Calibrationconfidence matches
North star: delayed performance per minute of practice.

patch.title: Define the finish line before studying
patch.content:
Replace “understand this” with: After seven days, without notes, I can…

  • reconstruct the key model or procedure;
  • explain why each step is necessary;
  • choose it over a nearby alternative;
  • solve one unfamiliar case.
Decision rule: if success cannot be scored, the target is still too vague.

patch.title: Retrieval is reconstruction—not recognition
patch.content:
Seeing an answer raises familiarity; producing it strengthens later access. Start with a blank page and a specific cue. Rebuild the explanation, diagram, derivation, or solution before opening the source.

Cue
→
Reconstruct
→
Compare

Diagnostic: obvious while visible but absent when hidden = recognition without reliable retrieval.

patch.title: Spacing works through useful forgetting
patch.content:
Waiting lets access weaken enough that recall requires reconstruction. The next review should be effortful but still possible.

Easy + completeLengthen the interval
Slow / partialRepeat the interval
WrongRepair now; retry sooner

Intervals are feedback-controlled—not sacred dates.

patch.title: Feedback repairs the model
patch.content:
Commit before checking. Compare your reasoning with a trusted solution and locate the first point of divergence.

missing linkmisconceptionwrong methodslipcue dependence

Write the smallest corrective rule, then test it on a fresh case. Copying the solution does not demonstrate repair.

patch.title: Sleep supports learning; it does not rescue it
patch.content:
Separate two claims: insufficient sleep can impair encoding before study; post-learning sleep may support retention and reorganization.

Average restriction effectg = 0.29

If immediate learning is weak, repair encoding first. Protect ordinary sleep opportunity; avoid consumer-device “deep sleep” targets, REM hacks, and audio recipes without task-specific evidence.

Entry condition: if no coherent attempt is possible, study a worked example first. Stopping rule: pass a delayed criterion twice under varied cues.

patch.title: Control the loop, not the calendar
patch.content:
Correct + easyIncrease delay or task variation
Correct + effortfulKeep or modestly increase delay
IncorrectClassify, repair, and shorten delay
Two failuresAdd a cue or worked example
High confidence missAudit fluency and calibration

patch.title: One 35-minute LASTS session
patch.content:
1. Locate · 3 min — define the no-notes target.
  2. Attempt · 7 min — solve, explain, or draw cold.
  3. Study gaps · 10 min — inspect only missing links.
  4. Test · 10 min — close everything and rebuild.
  5. Switch · 5 min — vary the case, log errors, schedule.
Output: one retrieval artifact, one repaired error, one follow-up—not passive notes.

patch.title: Adaptive spacing scheduler
patch.content:
Seed only: 1 → 3 → 7 → 14 → 30 days. Adjust after every attempt.

No cuesAdvance one interval
Slow / incompleteRepeat current interval
Needed hintMove back one interval
MisconceptionContrast models, then reschedule

Review the weakest dependency—not always the whole topic.

patch.title: Train the decision, not just the answer
patch.content:
Blocked practice asks, “Can I execute this method?” Interleaving also asks, “Can I recognize when it applies?”

  • change surface details and cue wording;
  • mix near-neighbor problem types;
  • name the method before solving;
  • explain the feature that selected it.
Boundary: mix methods only after basic execution is minimally stable.

patch.title: Five falsifiable mastery gates
patch.content:
Recall — reconstruct after a meaningful delay.
Mechanism — explain required causal links.
Discrimination — choose among nearby methods.
Transfer — solve changed surface details.
Calibration — confidence tracks performance.

Completion: pass at least four gates on two separated attempts. A failed gate defines the next practice task.

48,478students
222studies
g .499mean effect

Corrective feedback, repetition, format match, timing, control activity, and study design moderated outcomes. The mean is not a guaranteed gain.

EvidenceClassroom meta-analysis

Yang et al., 2021

Repeated study won at 5 minutes; retrieval practice won after 2 days and 1 week. Rereading also inflated confidence—an immediate-fluency illusion.

Boundary2 lab experiments · prose

Decision: evaluate a method with a closed-book test after a meaningful delay.

Roediger & Karpicke, 2006

d .54classroom mean
31effects
I² 92%heterogeneity

Distributed practice helps on average, but useful gaps depend on the desired retention horizon. Inverted-U evidence rejects both immediate and excessively delayed review.

Cepeda et al., 2008 · Mawson & Kang, 2025

Retrieval transfer is positive on average but moderated by response match, elaboration, initial performance, and transfer distance. Practiced access does not automatically become broad knowledge.

EvidenceTransfer meta-analysis

Diagnostic: change both cue and response format.

Pan & Rickard, 2018

Sleep restriction modestly impairs memory formation. Coordinated oscillations, reduced interference, and synaptic reorganization are more defensible than stage-specific consumer hacks.

node.title: First classify the learning target
node.content:
Label the target before choosing practice:

Fact / associationRecall cue
Explanation / modelCausal reconstruction
Procedure / skillPerformance + feedback
Judgment / transferCase discrimination

A flashcard can test the first; it cannot by itself validate the others.

node.title: Fluency audit: did study only feel productive?
node.content:
• Did I produce anything before seeing the answer?
  • Was there enough delay to require reconstruction?
  • Did feedback identify a reasoning failure?
  • Did I test a changed example?
  • Could I perform after cues disappeared?

Highlighting, rereading, and watching solutions may support encoding—but they are not mastery evidence.

node.title: Successive relearning is the operational core
node.content:
Retrieve correctly, return in later spaced sessions, and again practice until correct. This couples successful retrieval with spacing and makes accuracy—not exposure—the stopping criterion.

1correct recall now
+later sessions
d 1.5–4.2study effects
Reach one success, then leave. Another-day retrieval often beats same-session overlearning.

node.title: Difficulty is desirable only when it produces updating
node.content:
Harder is not automatically better. Unsupported retrieval can become guessing when knowledge or working-memory capacity is insufficient.

Coherent attemptRetrieve cold, then correct
Two failuresAdd a cue or worked example
No next-session gainRepair encoding, not difficulty

Fade support after success.

node.title: Error ledger: convert failure into a reusable asset
node.content:
Prompt + confidence — what did I believe?
Failure class — gap, model, selection, slip, cue?
First divergence — where did reasoning break?
Corrective rule — what cue changes the action?
Fresh test — does the repair generalize?

Repeated classes reveal what to change in the learning process.

node.title: Learning Bayes’ theorem through the loop
node.content:
Target: after seven days, calculate a posterior and explain why base rates matter.

Cold attempt1% prevalence, 90% sensitivity, 5% false-positive rate. Estimate P(disease | positive).
RepairAmong 10,000 people: 90 true positives, 495 false positives. Posterior = 90 ÷ 585 ≈ 15.4%.
TransferRepeat at 10% prevalence; predict the direction before calculating.
DiscriminateExplain why sensitivity alone cannot answer the question.

node.title: Better access is not yet broader knowledge
node.content:
Retrieval may strengthen practiced cue–response operations, add routes through related knowledge, or update remembered context. These accounts predict different transfer.

Test: change both the cue and the response format. Same-cue gain shows better access; cross-cue gain is stronger evidence of a more usable representation.

node.title: Measure the system, not study volume
node.content:
DAdelayed accuracy
CIcue independence
CGcalibration gap
  • Delayed accuracy: correct after the real interval.
  • Cue independence: correct under changed prompts.
  • Calibration gap: confidence minus performance.
  • Repair rate: failed gate passed next session.

Do not optimize streaks, cards reviewed, or hours logged.

node.title: Spaced success can override weak initial scheduling
node.content:
Across two experiments, successive relearning produced very large advantages over single-session learning (d = 1.52–4.19). Later relearning also shrank benefits from extra initial overlearning.

BoundaryTime and exposure differ by design
